To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dietary fat source (saturated, monounsaturated, n-6 polyunsaturated and n-3 polyunsaturated) and cholesterol level (0% and 2%) alter plasma lipids, tissue susceptibility to glutahione depletion and in vitro oxidation of plasma lipoprotein and tissue lipids.
the dietary fat source and level of dietary cholesterol interact to influence plasma lipid levels and tissue susceptibility to lipid peroxidation.

dietary fat blends of saturated, polyunsaturated, or monounsaturated fat and cholesterol do not affect blood pressure in spontaneously hypertensive rats, but they do affect plasma lipoprotein and tissue susceptibility to lipid peroxidation.

the effects of dietary fat and cholesterol on the susceptibility of LDL and tissue to oxidative stress in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs) and normotensives Wistar Kyoto ( WKY ) rats.
the effects of dietary fat sources and cholesterol on the development of hypertension, plasma lipoprotein and tissue oxidizability in spontaneously hypertensive rats.
the role that dietary fats play in modulating the development of hypertension, atherosclerosis, and oxidative damage to lipids and tissues.

the dietary fat source and the dietary cholesterol interact to influence plasma lipids, LDL and tissue antioxidant status and susceptibility to oxidation in SHR and WKy rats.

a moderate level of n-3 fat and high dietary cholesterol may have a protective effect on LDL and selected tissue susceptibility to oxidation.

a moderate amount of n-3 fatty acids in the diet can reduce tissue susceptibility to oxidation and LDL in vitro oxidation.
